title: I/O models
scopeHtml: Scope: blocking, non-blocking, select/poll/epoll, event loops (Nginx, Redis), zero-copy, io_uring and debugging. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: The I/O problem: waiting is the cost
notes.html:
Most server programs spend nearly all their time waiting for I/O (network, disk), not computing. A CPU does a billion simple steps per second; a network round trip inside a data centre takes about 0.5 ms, which is 500,000 CPU cycles of idleness. The question of "I/O models" is: what does the thread do while it waits?

Numbers worth remembering:

Operation Typical time
L1 cache hit 1 ns
RAM access 100 ns
Syscall (cheap) 100 to 500 ns
Context switch 2 to 5 microseconds
NVMe SSD read 20 to 100 microseconds
Same-datacentre round trip 500 microseconds
HDD seek 5 to 10 ms
Cross-continent round trip 80 to 150 ms

Five classic models (Stevens' UNIX Network Programming):

  1. Blocking I/O
  2. Non-blocking I/O (polling)
  3. I/O multiplexing (select, poll, epoll)
  4. Signal-driven I/O (rare)
  5. Asynchronous I/O (io_uring, Windows IOCP)

Worked example. A server must handle 10,000 connected clients, each sending a small request every 10 s, so about 1,000 requests/s. Each takes 50 microseconds of CPU (5% of one core). The CPU work is tiny; the challenge is managing 10,000 mostly idle sockets. That is the C10K problem (Dan Kegel, 1999). The thread-per-connection answer needs 10,000 threads; the multiplexing answer needs one.

Industry examples. Apache's classic prefork model used one process per connection and hit C10K; Nginx (2004) was written specifically to solve it with an event loop; Node.js, Redis, Netty, Envoy, HAProxy and Go's netpoller all follow the event-driven approach.

Everyday analogy. A waiter who stands at one table until the guests finish their meal (blocking) versus a waiter who moves among many tables and serves whoever is ready (event loop).

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up non-blocking with asynchronous. Non-blocking: the call returns immediately with "not ready". Asynchronous: you submit the operation and are told when it is complete.
  • Quoting C10K without saying what changed (event APIs plus cheap per-connection memory).

notes.title: Blocking I/O and thread-per-connection
notes.html:
With blocking I/O, read() puts the calling thread to sleep until data arrives. Simple code, one thread per connection:

ServerSocket ss = new ServerSocket(8080);
while (true) {
    Socket s = ss.accept();                  // blocks
    new Thread(() -> {
        try (var in = s.getInputStream()) {
            byte[] buf = new byte[4096];
            int n = in.read(buf);            // blocks until bytes arrive
            ...
        }
    }).start();
}

When the thread sleeps the CPU runs someone else, so it is not wasteful of CPU; it is wasteful of memory and scheduler work. Each Linux thread reserves a stack (Java default 1 MB virtual, 8 MB for main thread in C) plus kernel structures (~10 KB). 10,000 threads means about 10 GB of virtual address space, 100+ MB real, and the scheduler deals with thousands of runnable entities, so context switches climb.

Worked example. Tomcat default maximum 200 worker threads (Spring Boot server.tomcat.threads.max=200). If each request calls a database taking 100 ms, throughput caps at 200 / 0.1 = 2,000 requests/s regardless of CPU. If the DB slows to 1 s, the cap drops to 200 requests/s and the rest queue (default accept queue 100): the thread pool is the bottleneck. Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency.

Modern revival. Java 21 virtual threads and Go goroutines make thread-per-request cheap again: the runtime parks the lightweight thread on a blocking call and uses an event loop (epoll) underneath. You write blocking-style code with event-loop scalability. Goroutines start at about 2 to 8 KB of stack; a million is feasible.

Decision gravity. Thread-per-connection is the simplest to write and debug (stack traces make sense); the right default below a few thousand concurrent connections. Moving to an event loop is a rewrite of the I/O layer (one-way-ish); virtual threads let you keep the simple model.

Everyday analogy. Hiring one waiter per table. Easy to manage, but a restaurant with 10,000 tables cannot afford it.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking blocking threads burn CPU. They sleep; the cost is memory, stacks and scheduling.
  • Sizing the pool by CPU cores for I/O-bound work. Pool size for blocking work is about cores x (1 + wait/compute).

notes.title: Non-blocking I/O
notes.html:
A non-blocking socket (O_NONBLOCK) makes read() return immediately with the error EAGAIN (or EWOULDBLOCK) if no data is ready. The thread can then do something else. By itself that leads to busy-polling: loop over all sockets asking "ready yet?", burning CPU.

int flags = fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0);
fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK);
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
if (n < 0 && errno == EAGAIN) { /* nothing yet, do other work */ }

Polling 10,000 sockets with 10,000 read calls takes 10,000 syscalls x ~300 ns = 3 ms per sweep, nearly all returning EAGAIN. Useless without a way to ask the kernel "which of these are ready?". That is I/O multiplexing.

Non-blocking also matters for connect (returns EINPROGRESS, completion signalled as writable) and accept. Note: regular disk files are always "ready", so O_NONBLOCK does nothing for them; epoll cannot wait on disk files. This is why Node.js uses a thread pool (libuv) for file I/O, and why io_uring matters.

Everyday analogy. Checking the oven door every second instead of setting a timer.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing O_NONBLOCK works for regular files.
  • Forgetting to loop read until EAGAIN when using edge-triggered epoll.

notes.title: select, poll and epoll
notes.html:
I/O multiplexing lets one thread block on many file descriptors at once and wake up when any is ready.

select (1983): pass three bitmaps (read, write, error) of up to FD_SETSIZE = 1024 descriptors. On return, the kernel has overwritten the bitmaps, so you rebuild them every call, and you scan all of them to find the ready ones. Cost O(n) per call, copying n entries each time.

poll: array of struct pollfd, no 1024 limit, still O(n) per call (copy the whole array to the kernel and scan it).

epoll (Linux 2.6, 2002): three calls.

  • epoll_create1() makes an epoll instance in the kernel.
  • epoll_ctl(ADD | MOD | DEL, fd, event) registers interest once. The kernel keeps a red-black tree of watched fds and a ready list.
  • epoll_wait() returns only the ready ones: cost O(ready), not O(watched).
int ep = epoll_create1(0);
struct epoll_event ev = { .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = listen_fd };
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd, &ev);
struct epoll_event ready[256];
for (;;) {
    int n = epoll_wait(ep, ready, 256, -1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) handle(ready[i].data.fd);
}

Level-triggered vs edge-triggered. Level (default): epoll_wait keeps reporting a fd as long as data remains unread. Edge (EPOLLET): reports once when data arrives; you must read until EAGAIN or you lose wake-ups. Edge reduces wake-ups but is easier to get wrong. Use EPOLLEXCLUSIVE or SO_REUSEPORT to avoid a thundering herd when several workers wait on the same listen socket.

Worked example. 10,000 connections, only 50 active at a time. select/poll: each loop copies and scans 10,000 entries, roughly 10,000 x ~20 ns = 200 microseconds of pure overhead per wake-up. epoll: returns 50 entries, about 2 microseconds. At 50,000 wake-ups per second that is 10 s of CPU per second for poll (impossible on one core) versus 0.1 s for epoll.

Platform equivalents. BSD and macOS: kqueue. Windows: IOCP (a completion model). Java NIO Selector uses epoll on Linux. Android's Looper message loop waits in native epoll_wait.

Decision gravity. Use the library (libuv, Netty, tokio, libevent) rather than raw epoll; the event-loop model forces never block the loop: one slow handler stalls every connection on that thread. Reversible at library boundary; architecture around callbacks or async/await is sticky.

Everyday analogy. A hotel front desk: instead of calling each room to ask "do you need anything?", rooms press a button and a board lights up only the ones that want service.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying epoll is "faster at I/O". It is faster at finding ready descriptors; with few, busy connections poll is just as good.
  • Doing a blocking call (DB query, Thread.sleep, big JSON parse) in an event-loop thread.
  • Forgetting epoll does not support regular files.

notes.title: The event loop in practice: why Nginx and Redis are fast
notes.html:
One thread (or one per core), no locks, never blocking, handling thousands of connections via epoll.

Nginx. A master process spawns worker processes (worker_processes auto; = one per core). Each worker runs its own event loop over thousands of connections, with a small state machine per connection (a few KB). No thread per connection, no shared locks between workers (the kernel balances accepts via SO_REUSEPORT or an accept mutex). A static file is served with sendfile (zero-copy, see below).

worker_processes auto;
events { worker_connections 20000; use epoll; }
http { sendfile on; tcp_nopush on; keepalive_timeout 30; }

With 4 workers x 20,000 connections, one box holds 80,000 concurrent connections in a few hundred MB of RAM. An Apache prefork server at 10 MB per process would need 800 GB.

Redis. Command execution is single-threaded: one thread runs an event loop (its own ae library over epoll). Why that is fast:

  • Data lives in RAM; commands are microsecond operations (GET about 1 to 2 microseconds of CPU).
  • No locks, no context switches, perfect cache locality.
  • Each command is atomic for free (no concurrent mutation of data structures).
  • The bottleneck becomes the network, about 100,000 to 200,000 ops/s on one core without pipelining, over 1 million with pipelining.

Since Redis 6, optional I/O threads (io-threads 4) parse and write sockets in parallel, while command execution stays single-threaded. Redis 8 and Valkey improved this further.

The catch: slow commands block everyone. KEYS * on 10 million keys, SMEMBERS of a huge set, or a Lua script running 50 ms stalls every client for 50 ms.

$ redis-cli --latency
min: 0, max: 1, avg: 0.12 (1832 samples)
$ redis-cli slowlog get 3
1) 1) (integer) 14
   2) (integer) 1731000000
   3) (integer) 182340        # microseconds: a 182 ms command blocked the server
   4) 1) "KEYS" 2) "*"

Use SCAN (incremental), and UNLINK instead of DEL for huge keys (frees memory in a background thread).

Industry examples. Node.js (libuv), Netty, Envoy, HAProxy, Memcached (a few threads with epoll), Vert.x, Python asyncio, Rust tokio, and Go's runtime netpoller (epoll under goroutines).

Everyday analogy. One fast chef who never waits: the chef never stands watching a pot; as soon as a timer rings they handle that dish, so one chef serves many tables. But if the chef takes a 10-minute phone call, everyone waits.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Redis is fast "because it is in memory" only. Also single-threaded design, simple data structures, and an efficient protocol (RESP).
  • Believing Redis is entirely single-threaded. Background threads exist (lazy free, AOF fsync, I/O threads in v6+).
  • Running CPU-heavy work in a Node event loop; use worker threads.

notes.title: Zero-copy I/O
notes.html:
Normal file-to-socket transfer copies data four times and crosses user/kernel boundary twice. read(file_fd, buf) then write(sock_fd, buf):

1. Disk -> kernel page cache      (DMA)
2. Page cache -> user buffer      (CPU copy)  <- wasted
3. User buffer -> socket buffer   (CPU copy)  <- wasted
4. Socket buffer -> NIC           (DMA)
Plus 2 syscalls and 2 context switches.

sendfile(out_fd, in_fd, offset, count) tells the kernel to move data directly from the page cache to the socket: no copy into user space, one syscall. With NIC scatter-gather DMA, even the copy into the socket buffer is skipped (only descriptors are passed), giving "true" zero-copy: the CPU copies zero bytes.

Related tools:

  • mmap: map a file into your address space; reads page-fault from the cache. Saves one copy, but page faults and TLB cost; error handling on truncated files is awkward (SIGBUS).
  • splice / tee: move data between a pipe and an fd inside the kernel.
  • MSG_ZEROCOPY (Linux 4.14): zero-copy send for large buffers (worth it above about 10 KB; completion notifications make it clumsy for small ones).
  • DPDK / kernel bypass / RDMA: the user program talks to the NIC directly; used in trading and some storage systems.
  • TLS caveat: encryption must read the data, so plain sendfile does not help unless kernel TLS (kTLS) is used (Nginx and Netflix's FreeBSD CDN do this).

Worked example. Serving a 1 GB video at 10 Gbit/s (1.25 GB/s). The copy path moves 1.25 GB/s through user space twice: about 2.5 GB/s of memcpy plus syscall overhead, consuming roughly one to two cores. With sendfile the CPU mostly idles; one core can fill a 10 Gbit link. Netflix Open Connect appliances serve over 100 Gbit/s per box using sendfile plus kTLS on FreeBSD (Netflix has published about 400 Gbit/s per server).

Industry examples. Kafka's consumer fetch path uses sendfile (via Java FileChannel.transferTo) so reading from disk to the consumer socket never touches the JVM heap, one reason a Kafka broker serves many consumers cheaply. Nginx sendfile on;. Apache EnableSendfile.

Decision gravity. Use sendfile for static content and log streaming without transformation; once you must modify data (compress, encrypt in user space), it no longer applies. Reversible config.

Everyday analogy. Instead of a courier carrying a parcel into your office and then to the post box, the post-room hands the parcel straight to the post van.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming zero-copy means no copies at all. The DMA transfers still happen; it means zero CPU copies between user and kernel.
  • Forgetting TLS and compression defeat the plain sendfile path.

notes.title: io_uring
notes.html:
io_uring (Linux 5.1, 2019, by Jens Axboe) is a true asynchronous I/O interface built on two shared ring buffers between user space and kernel. You write requests into the submission queue (SQ); the kernel writes results into the completion queue (CQ). Because the rings are shared memory, you can submit many operations and collect many completions with zero or one syscalls (io_uring_enter), or even zero syscalls with SQPOLL (a kernel thread polls the SQ).

// liburing sketch: read 4 KB asynchronously
struct io_uring ring; io_uring_queue_init(256, &ring, 0);
struct io_uring_sqe *sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(&ring);
io_uring_prep_read(sqe, fd, buf, 4096, 0);
sqe->user_data = 42;
io_uring_submit(&ring);                     // one syscall for many sqes
struct io_uring_cqe *cqe; io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe);
printf("req %llu result %d\n", cqe->user_data, cqe->res);
io_uring_cqe_seen(&ring, cqe);

What it adds over epoll:

  • Real async disk I/O. epoll cannot wait on regular files; Linux's older AIO (libaio) only worked well with O_DIRECT. io_uring handles buffered files, sockets, accept, connect, send, recv, fsync, openat and more through one interface.
  • Batching: 32 operations, one syscall.
  • Fixed files and fixed buffers: pre-register fds and buffers to skip per-call lookups.
  • Linked operations: "read then write then fsync" as a chain.
  • Multishot accept/recv, provided buffers, and since 6.x, zero-copy send/receive.

Worked example. A storage service doing 1 million 4 KB random reads/s on NVMe. With blocking pread per thread you need many threads and ~1 million syscalls/s (about 0.3 s of CPU in syscall entry/exit alone, more with KPTI mitigations). With io_uring batching 64 at a time: ~16,000 submits/s, and SQPOLL can bring it to near zero. Reported results show single-core NVMe IOPS rising from ~400K to over a million.

Trade-offs and security. It is a big, young kernel attack surface: many container runtimes and Google (for ChromeOS and production) restricted or disabled io_uring after multiple privilege-escalation CVEs; Docker's default seccomp profile blocks it in newer releases (confirm for your version). Needs kernel 5.10+ for sane feature sets, 6.x for the newest ops. Programming model is more complex than epoll.

Industry examples. RocksDB and some databases experimented with it; ScyllaDB's Seastar has an io_uring backend; Rust runtimes (tokio-uring, glommio, monoio) and the liburing library; Node's libuv uses it for file ops in newer versions (confirm per release). Cloudflare, Meta have written about using it selectively.

Decision gravity. Choose io_uring when you need async disk I/O or extremely high syscall rates and control your kernel version; epoll remains the safe default for ordinary network servers. Medium reversibility: adds a platform dependency (Linux only).

Everyday analogy. Instead of phoning the kitchen for each order, you drop a stack of order slips on a shared counter and pick up finished plates from a second counter, without speaking.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying io_uring is just a faster epoll. It is a completion-based async interface, different in kind.
  • Ignoring the security posture (seccomp/blocked in many sandboxes).
  • Claiming epoll supports disk files.

notes.title: Choosing an I/O model and debugging it
notes.html:
Decision ladder.

Situation Choice
Under about 2,000 concurrent connections, simple team Blocking threads
Same code style, huge concurrency Virtual threads (Java 21) or goroutines
10K to 1M connections, mostly idle Event loop on epoll (Netty, Node, Nginx)
Heavy disk I/O async, newest kernels io_uring
Serving big static files sendfile (plus kTLS)
CPU-bound work in an event-driven server Hand off to a worker pool

Debugging toolkit (Linux).

$ ss -s                                   # socket totals
Total: 41234  TCP: 40112 (estab 38990, closed 120, timewait 118)
$ ss -ltn                                 # Recv-Q on a LISTEN socket = accept backlog waiting
State   Recv-Q  Send-Q  Local Address:Port
LISTEN  129     128     0.0.0.0:8080      # Recv-Q > Send-Q: accept queue FULL, app too slow
$ sudo strace -f -c -p 2310 -- sleep 5    # which syscalls dominate
% time  seconds  calls  syscall
 71.2   2.9      90210  epoll_wait
 20.1   0.8     310550  write
$ cat /proc/2310/limits | grep 'open files'
Max open files   1024   1048576   files      # raise nofile limit for C10K

Production patterns:

  • "Too many open files" (EMFILE): ulimit -n / LimitNOFILE=1048576 in systemd; one fd per socket.
  • Accept queue overflow: ss -ltn shows Recv-Q at the backlog (somaxconn, default 4096 on newer kernels, 128 on older). Symptom: clients see connect timeouts while CPU is idle. nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows counts drops.
  • Event loop lag: one thread at 100% CPU (top -H) while others idle; latency across all connections rises. Find the blocking handler with perf top or an application profiler.
  • Ephemeral port exhaustion on the client side: 28K ports by default (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range), many TIME_WAIT; use connection pooling and keep-alive.

Everyday analogy. A busy restaurant: check how many diners are queuing at the door (accept queue), whether the single chef is stuck (loop lag), and whether you ran out of table numbers (fds).

Common interview traps.

  • Raising thread pool sizes instead of finding the blocking call.
  • Not knowing where the connection backlog is visible (ss -ltn).
  • Treating the default ulimit -n 1024 as fine for a server.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• I/O is slow compared to CPU; the I/O model decides what a thread does while waiting. Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency.
  • Blocking + thread per connection is simplest; costs memory and context switches at C10K scale. Virtual threads and goroutines bring the model back cheaply.
  • Non-blocking returns EAGAIN; useless alone and does nothing for regular files.
  • select/poll are O(n) per call; epoll registers once and returns only ready fds. Level vs edge triggering; use SO_REUSEPORT or exclusive wake-ups.
  • Nginx (worker per core, event loop, sendfile) and Redis (single-threaded in-memory, no locks, atomic commands) are fast because of event loops plus no blocking; a slow command blocks everyone.
  • Zero-copy (sendfile, splice, MSG_ZEROCOPY) avoids CPU copies; TLS and transformation defeat the simple version unless kTLS is used.
  • io_uring is shared-ring async I/O for files and sockets with batching; powerful but young and often blocked in sandboxes.
  • Debug with ss -ltn, strace -c, top -H, fd limits and accept-queue counters.
